I'm aware this is a VR game from 2017 and in 2017 I probably would have rated it as good ... but, let's face it, once the initial fascination has worn off, you start looking at how much game there actually is. And in case of Form there's little beyond what you give toddlers or really young kids to play with. Fit a shape into the right hole, remember a sequence of four ... it's so low level and trivial that it takes more time to figure out what the game needs you to do than to actually do it. Yes, the visuals, music and sounds are nice, but it doesn't amount to anything beyond just that. it's very much like The Room games, just a lot less complex, but with the same bloated, non-sensical self-importance. So, an okay 80 minutes demo of VR with rather poor controls and a tiny bit of story tacked on that amounts to nothing. 3/10.

Form is the perfect game to introduce players to VR. The puzzles are all relatively simple to solve and don't require much, if any, coordination, so they give players time to get acquainted with the controls. The surreal environments are a fantastic and highlight the benefits of stereoscopic 3D. The movement is entirely teleportation based, so new players are less likely to get sick from movement as they adjust to other aspects of interacting in VR. The story is the main point that I found quite lacking. Overall, if you're a seasoned VR user, this game may not seem super relevant to you, but it is worth an hour of your time if you get it on sale or in a Humble Bundle. If you're new to VR or if you want to introduce a friend, this is a great puzzle game to get started with.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
FORM is pretty awesome. I don't know what this artstyle is called, the geometric, low-poly, edge-glow amalgamation that defines this game, but I've always had a softspot for the exact style and colors this game uses. It's definitely a game to vibe with.

Artstyle aside, the soundtrack is neat, lots of noise going on though so I didn't get to sit down and wow at it (there is a dedicated mode for this, I've yet to try it, but certainly will because the ambient tracks were awesome).

For the price? Not so hot. I could see this game being a smidge cheaper considering its length (I finished it in a single 52 minute sitting). I'd see $5 as a steal and $10 as about right.

The developer side of myself looks at this game as it if were technical implementation. It was missing that "finalized" feel to it. The development team gives me the vibe that they were tinkering with mechanics and put them into a housing that allowed them to showcase these mechanics in a manner digestible to the consumer.

[h1]Issues[/h1]
I have no complaints aside from price/length. I got it on sale so I'm happy, but I would be a bit peeved if this is what I got at full price.

[h1]Suggestions & Feedback - What would fix the issues?[/h1]
Well, I can say that "longer game" is a [i]horrible[/i] answer at face value - these puzzle mechanics would get terribly boring if it were any longer, and it'd undoubtedly turn the image of the game for the worse. There's a different angle of attack to take that inadvertently satisfies the "longer game" desire, and I personally think this is the way to go right here: Make it into a story that is told as the player goes through the game, intermittently swapping between storytelling and interaction. Take a look at a title like Quantum Break for example. Use a storytelling mechanic like that and this game will shoot straight into the stars.

[h1]So should I get it?[/h1]
Get it during the summer sale when the price is (ideally) put at 50% or less.
